Q: Where can I find all the dependencies specified by Spring Boot's bill of materials? A:

This is listed in the Spring Boot documentation under Dependency Versions. More specifically, in Managed Dependency Coordinates.

Alternatively, consult the Maven BOM (org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies) of your Spring Boot version.

Q: Why are double brackets required? A:

Assigned() is a compiler intrinsic that expects a variable passed by var reference, but TValue.AsObject is not a variable, it is a function that returns an rvalue. You can't pass an rvalue to a var parameter, hence the "variable required" error.

However, by including the extra parenthesis, the compiler has to evaluate the rvalue and is able to then optimize if not Assigned ((Value.AsObject)) then into basically being if Value.AsObject() = nil then. There is no actual function call to Assigned().

Q: Can I make MyDAC update a blob field faster? A:

In general you would use a relational database to store structured data. Things like names, ages, positions, locations, quantities, etc. These are small data items. Not 50MB. Anything that's more than a few KB is better stored in the file system. Think of things like images, signals, PDFs, etc.

In the end a relational database, of course, also uses the file system, but it comes with its own overhead. Your blob has to become part of a database file. When you perform an update command, the old blob needs to be removed, and the new blob appended. The database file might be quite huge, you probably have many big blobs stored in it, making these operations slow. Other database files probably also need updating as well, like the index files. If you perform more than one operation on the same database table your program might also have to wait for the previous operation to finish.

By storing larger chunks of data directly into the file system you can speeds things up quite a bit, especially when the file system uses caching for write actions. You can also look at this another way: The file system is also a kind of database, but it can efficiently handle larger chunks of data.

The file system uses the hierarchical database model, each item is only linked to one parent, instead of the more complex relational database model where items are linked to rows and columns of tables.

Q: What are the benefits of using = instead of LIKE in SQL? A:

A personal example using mysql 5.5: I had an inner join between 2 tables, one of 3 million rows and one of 10 thousand rows.

Q: Visual Studio Debugging: freeze current thread by code A:

Freezing a given thread programmatically is not much of problem. You can have the thread wait on a synchronization object of choice(e.g std::mutex). The problem is signaling the sync object via an external tool like the debugger.

But, you can write a we simple debug assistant program with limited options, that loads and runs the subject program. The two processes can negotiate through a named OS specific interprocess semaphore.

If you want the IDE to control an watch the variables, you can have the debug assistant run separately. What connects the subject and assistant is a named semaphore that subject threads block on, and you can control the assistant in a separate command line terminal via console.

Q: Retry async/await try and catch block three times before responding with an error A:

For the simplest solution, without involving any extra library, simply borrow the retryAsync function from this repo, and then just replace one line in your code as shown below...

Replace

await myAsyncFunction(body)

With

await retryAsync(() => myAsyncFunction(body), {retry: 3})

Above, we say:

Here's a Promise-returning function that we want tried up to 3 times before rejecting.

This way, your original code can be reduced to just:

router.post('/', async function (req, res) {
    try {
        await retryAsync(() => myAsyncFunction(body), {retry: 3})
        res.json({ success: true, message: 'Done!' })
    } catch (err) {
        res.json({ success: false, message: err && err.message })
    }
}

Q: Couldn't upgrade SQL Server LocalDB to 2022 version A:

I've solved the problem by following this page https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/configure-windows/sql-server-express-localdb?view=sql-server-ver16

  • Run SQL2022-SSEI-Expr.exe then choose "download media" and click localdb on the specified download location.
  • You will see a file called SqlLocalDB.msi - run and and install it.
